notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on force majeure and contract certainty in oil supply disputes.

enrichment.short_title: Force majeure defence rejected where FYROM government letters instigated by Okta to avoid Jetoil contract
key_facts: Jetoil held a 1993 English-law contract giving exclusive crude oil handling rights and first refusal at Okta's Skopje refinery until March 2003.
From July 1999 Okta admitted breaching the contract after Hellenic Petroleum gained influence through privatisation.
Okta relied on FYROM government letters of November 1999 and May 2001 requesting non-performance under a force majeure clause covering compliance with governmental requests.
Aikens J found the letters were requests but that Okta had instigated them and its non-performance was not attributable to them.
In a second action, Moil-Coal claimed under a 1998 oil supply contract; Okta argued the pricing clause was too uncertain.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from two Commercial Court judgments of Aikens J on breach of contract and contract validity.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals dismissed; force majeure defence rejected and the 1998 oil supply contract held enforceable.
enrichment.ratio: A force majeure clause excusing failure attributable to a governmental request beyond the party's control does not apply where the party itself instigated the request rather than complying with its contractual obligations; a pricing mechanism need not be perfectly precise if the parties operated the contract and a court or broker could resolve disputes.
legal_issues: Whether FYROM government letters activated the force majeure clause
Whether Okta instigated requests that were beyond its control
Whether failure to give prompt force majeure notice barred reliance
Whether the 1998 pricing clause rendered the oil supply contract unenforceable for uncertainty

notes: Complete second appeal on construction of section 20 Leasehold Reform Act 1993.

enrichment.short_title: Office copy register entries sufficed for section 20 title deduction despite pre-relevant-date certification

statutes_considered.title: Leasehold Reform, Housing and Urban Development Act 1993
Leasehold Reform (Collective Enfranchisement and Lease Renewal) Regulations 1993 (SI 1993/2407)

key_facts: Belle Vue Gardens Ltd served section 13 initial notices on 6 August 2001 for collective enfranchisement of three Bournemouth flat blocks.
Raymere Ltd served section 20 notices requiring title deduction within 21 days.
The nominee purchaser supplied office copy entries certified as subsisting on 12 June 2001, eight weeks before the relevant date.
Raymere contended this did not conclusively prove title as at 6 August 2001 and that initial notices were deemed withdrawn under section 20(3).
It was common ground that the register had not changed between the certification date and the relevant date.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal to the Court of Appeal from county court decisions dismissing Raymere's claim for declarations that section 20 notices had not been complied with.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; supplying timely office copy entries constituted compliance with section 20 even though certification predated the relevant date.
enrichment.ratio: Section 20 requires an administrative procedural response to deduce title supporting the initial notice, not conclusive proof of good title as at the relevant date; imperfect but good-faith compliance does not trigger deemed withdrawal, and title defects should be raised in a section 21 counter-notice or section 22 proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether section 20 requires title deduced as at the relevant date
Whether office copy entries with an earlier certification date constitute compliance
Whether section 21(2)(b) informs the construction of section 20
Whether non-compliance triggers deemed withdrawal under section 20(3)

notes: Complete planning injunction appeal following South Bucks v Porter.

enrichment.short_title: Planning injunction wording broadened to restrain repair workshop use while preserving ancillary shop fitting

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order 1995

key_facts: Mr Dowman operated a motor spares shop at 572 North Circular Road, Neasden; an enforcement notice required cessation of unauthorised use as a car repair workshop.
The inspector upheld the notice in 1995; Dowman continued in breach and was convicted.
Brent sought a section 187B injunction; the judge granted one listing specific prohibited repair activities but omitting others such as engine testing and servicing.
Dowman argued established mixed use including minor repairs; the council accepted ancillary fitting to shop sales.
The council preferred a general order restraining use as a repair workshop subject to an ancillary-fitting exception.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against the terms of a county court injunction granted under section 187B Town and Country Planning Act 1990.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; injunction reframed in general terms restraining use as a repair workshop while permitting fitting ancillary to retail shop use; no equipment-removal order.
enrichment.ratio: A section 187B injunction should not normally restrain uses ancillary to a permitted primary use or permitted development; a landowner cannot at committal stage reopen established-use rights that should have been raised on a section 174 appeal, but imprecise general wording may be appropriate where ancillary use disputes are inevitable.
legal_issues: Whether the injunction should use a list or general formulation
Whether Dowman could rely on established mixed use at the injunction stage
Whether ancillary shop-fitting activities should be excluded
Whether equipment removal should be ordered

notes: Complete appeal reversing summary judgment on proprietary estoppel occupation claim.

enrichment.short_title: Summary judgment set aside where Mrs Clibbery raised arguable proprietary estoppel to occupy The Gables
key_facts: Century SA (UK) Ltd owned The Gables, a large Newmarket property managed for Ivan Allan, who invited Mrs Clibbery to live there from 1987 on assurance she could stay as long as she wished.
Mrs Clibbery ran the house and performed unpaid duties; after Allan's relationship with her daughter broke down, the company sought possession.
Mrs Clibbery defended claiming proprietary estoppel; a deputy master found a fragile estoppel case but a deputy judge allowed the company's summary judgment appeal.
On appeal, the court held there was an arguable proprietary estoppel claim and that Allan acted as the company's agent when granting occupation.
The constructive trust claim was abandoned in favour of a non-exclusive licence for life based on proprietary estoppel.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from a deputy High Court judge's decision allowing summary judgment for possession under CPR Part 24.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; summary judgment set aside and matter remitted for full trial on proprietary estoppel.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant asserts an assurance of indefinite occupation and detriment by unpaid house management, summary judgment is inappropriate even if the claim faces serious difficulties at trial; the agent/principal point as to who granted the licence can be determined on the summary application if clear on the evidence.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Clibbery had an arguable proprietary estoppel claim
Whether the deputy judge erred in treating assistance as insufficient detriment
Whether the claim was proprietary estoppel rather than constructive trust
Whether Ivan Allan granted the licence on behalf of the company

notes: Complete administrative court appeal from Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal suspension.

enrichment.short_title: Six-month suspension upheld for solicitor who backdated legal aid franchise compliance documents
key_facts: Mr Loader, a salaried partner at Martin Cray and Co, admitted inserting backdated client care letters and file review forms into legal aid files before a 1995 franchise audit.
He accepted the conduct involved deception of the Legal Aid Board though actual client care was not deficient.
The Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal imposed a six-month suspension for conscious impropriety; junior solicitors received reprimands.
Loader appealed alleging procedural unfairness because the Tribunal relied on his 1997 witness statement blaming Mr Cray, and alleging disproportionate penalty and delay.
The court found the Tribunal sentenced on the agreed basis of plea and did not treat the 1997 statement as an aggravating factor.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Administrative Court appeal by case stated from a Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal decision imposing suspension.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; six-month suspension from 1 August 2003 upheld; Law Society costs summarily assessed at £14,000.
enrichment.ratio: A disciplinary tribunal may assess the truth of a witness statement when deciding another respondent's case but cannot use adverse findings on that statement against a respondent who pleaded on an agreed basis without giving him opportunity to answer; conscious impropriety by an experienced solicitor warrants suspension even where deception was at the lower end of gravity.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal departed from the agreed basis of plea
Whether reliance on the April 1997 statement was procedurally unfair
Whether the six-month suspension was disproportionate compared with junior colleagues
Whether delay required a lesser penalty

notes: Complete pension scheme construction appeal with split court on compulsory redundancy.

enrichment.short_title: Pension rule covered voluntary but not compulsory redundancy for unreduced early retirement at 50
key_facts: AGCO closed its Coventry Banner Lane tractor plant, making most Massey Ferguson pension scheme members redundant.
Rule 13(c)(iii) of the Works and Staff Schemes entitled members over 50 who retire from service at the request of the employer to an immediate unreduced normal retirement pension.
Neuberger J held both voluntary and compulsory redundancy and other dismissals fell within the rule.
The employer argued redundancy is dismissal, not retirement at the employer's request; employees argued all redundancies qualify.
The Court of Appeal (majority) held voluntary redundancy is consensual retirement at the employer's request but compulsory redundancy is not.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from a Part 8 declaration of Neuberger J on construction of pension scheme rules.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; declarations amended so compulsory redundancy and most other dismissals fall outside rule 13(c)(iii), but voluntary redundancy accepted and invited by the employer qualifies.
enrichment.ratio: In pension scheme rules, retire at the request of the employer naturally covers consensual early retirement and voluntary redundancy but not compulsory dismissal; retirement is used intransitively and request implies the employee may choose, whereas compulsory redundancy is an enforced dismissal even if formally executed by notice.
legal_issues: Whether redundancy amounts to retiring from service at the request of the employer
Whether voluntary and compulsory redundancy should be treated differently
Whether dismissals for misconduct fall within rule 13(c)(iii)
The 50/60 age anomaly between rules 13(c)(ii) and (iii)

notes: Complete Commercial Court judgment on Hatfield rail disaster business interruption insurance.

enrichment.short_title: Hatfield ESR losses covered only for restrictions before policy expiry; wear-and-tear exclusion inapplicable
key_facts: National Express train operating companies claimed business interruption losses after the Hatfield derailment of 17 October 2000 caused network-wide emergency speed restrictions.
Policies with CGNU and St Paul covered denial of access when the insured was prevented from or hindered in use of the rail network by action of a competent authority for public safety.
Railtrack imposed hundreds of ESRs across the network over many months following GCC inspections; cover expired on 31 October 2000.
Insurers argued each ESR was a separate occurrence and only pre-expiry restrictions were covered; claimants argued one composite Railtrack Programme event.
St Paul policy special conditions excluded restrictions not consequent upon damage to infrastructure and continuing post-reinstatement restrictions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of preliminary issues of construction on business interruption insurance claims following Hatfield.
enrichment.outcome: Each ESR was a separate occurrence; only losses from restrictions imposed before 31 October 2000 are covered under CGNU; wear-and-tear exclusion does not apply but St Paul special condition 2(ii) excludes most ESR losses; deductibles may be aggregated by reference to the derailment event.
enrichment.ratio: Under a denial-of-access extension, the insured peril is hindrance in use of track caused by competent authority action, not the authority's decision alone; individual ESRs lack unity of time and place and are separate occurrences; rolling contact fatigue is wear and tear but ESR imposition was the proximate cause of loss; St Paul condition 2(ii) requires restrictions proximately caused by physical damage to infrastructure.
legal_issues: Construction of the denial of access clause occurrence
Whether ESRs form one occurrence or multiple events
Whether wear and tear / gradual deterioration exclusion applies
St Paul special conditions 2(ii) and 2(iii)
Deductible aggregation for series of losses from one event

key_facts: Mrs Taheri, an Iraqi refugee with limited English and mild to moderate depression, applied to Westminster as homeless with her husband.

notes: Complete appeal on normal retiring age under Employment Rights Act 1996 section 109.

enrichment.short_title: Customs Band 6 contractual retiring age of 62 defeated unfair-dismissal age bar at 60
key_facts: Mr Jayawardane, a Customs and Excise Band 6 executive officer born May 1940, was dismissed effective 30 November 2000 aged 60.
Customs argued section 109 excluded unfair dismissal claims because 60 was the normal retiring age for his position.
Staff handbook paragraph 1.2 stated Band 5 and 6 staff could not be required to leave before 62 unless compulsorily redundant.
The employment tribunal found contractual and normal retiring age was 62 without statistical evidence.
The EAT remitted the case, holding the tribunal conflated contractual and normal retiring age and misapplied Waite.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal decision remitting normal retiring age issue to a fresh tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; EAT order set aside and tribunal decision restored; normal retiring age held to be 62 so unfair dismissal claim may proceed.
enrichment.ratio: Where the contractual retiring age is 62 and no evidence shows employees regularly retire at a higher age, the normal retiring age for section 109 is 62; the tribunal may treat staff handbook provisions as contractual and need not first apply a reasonable-expectation test to determine contractual age when 62 is the age before which compulsory retirement is prohibited.
legal_issues: Distinction between contractual retiring age and normal retiring age under section 109
Whether staff handbook provisions fix contractual retiring age
Application of Lord Fraser's test in Waite v GCHQ
Relevance of retirement statistics

notes: Complete judicial review on young offender removal-from-unit punishment and ECHR claims.

enrichment.short_title: Young offender removal from unit breached YOI Rules but did not violate Articles 3 or 8
key_facts: BP, aged 17, was punished with removal from his wing to a segregation unit for five and then four days at Warren Hill YOI for disciplinary offences.
During removal he was deprived of education, training, work and physical education contrary to Rule 61(c) and Prison Service guidance.
He had a history of self-harm incidents but was medically cleared for the punishment.
He claimed Article 3 and Article 8 breaches and failure to investigate rape allegations at Hunterscombe.
The prison accepted the Rule breach and had begun changing the segregation regime to provide purposeful activity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of disciplinary removal-from-unit detention at Warren Hill young offender institution.
enrichment.outcome: Application allowed on YOI Rules breach but no relief granted; Article 3 and Article 8 claims rejected; rape-investigation claim refused as improperly raised; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Removal from wing under Rule 61(g) does not permit deprivation of compulsory education, training, work or physical education for under-18 trainees; that breach engages welfare principles from Howard League but does not without more attain Article 3 or Article 8 severity, particularly where the segregation conditions were disputed and no adverse psychological effect was evidenced.
legal_issues: Whether removal from unit unlawfully excluded mandatory regime activities
Whether conditions amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3
Whether detention violated Article 8 private life and physical integrity
Whether the Home Department failed to investigate rape allegations
